Health Dengue fever outbreak in Florida: Symptoms, number of cases and locations where the mosquito-borne illness is spreading Greg Heilman Update: Sep 29th, 2026 10:31 EDT 0 Share facebook twitter whatsapp Make us preferred on Google Florida is experiencing what one local official called a “wildly unusual” explosion of dengue infections. So far, there have been 392 dengue fever cases reported, both linked to travel and locally acquired, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The latter cases are of the most concern, with 190 cases of locally acquired dengue according to the most recent Florida Arbovirus Surveillance report and 17 mosquito pools in six counties. Hillsborough County is the county with the most reported cases, 177, in the Sunshine state followed by Miam-Dade County which has 132 reported cases according to the CDC. Local states of emergency have been declared in Hillsborough, home to Tampa Bay, as well as two neighboring counties, Pasco and Pinellas. This will allow them to coordinate resources more quickly to protect public health and ask for necessary funds and assistance from the state and federal government. CDC How is dengue transmitted? The Florida Department of Health says that dengue fever is “acquired through the bite of certain species of mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti, but also Aedes albopictus, both of which are present in Florida.” According to the latest Florida Arbovirus Surveillance report, six counties are under mosquito-borne illness advisories including Leon, Alachua, Brevard, Walton, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Walton. The counties of Duval, Hillsborough, Maimi-Dade, Orange, and Pinellas are under mosquito-borne illnesses alerts. Here’s the Aedes aegypti risk map from @eLife the entire Gulf of Mexico is at risk (Gulf of America too) from TX to FL that could mean not only the return of dengue, but also Zika, Chikungunya, attached are my concerns about yellow fever as well, it’s why we organized a school of... https://t.co/cdtIakzay1 pic.twitter.com/hpvKiWwgee — Prof Peter Hotez MD PhD DSc(hon) (@PeterHotez) September 29, 2026 What are the symptoms of dengue, aka “breakbone fever”? People who get infected with dengue can experience a “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”), and bleeding,” explains the Florida Department of Health. In some cases, those infected experience gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea. In rare cases, people can contract a more severe form of the infection, dengue hemorrhagic fever, “that can be fatal if not recognized and treated with supportive care.” Symptoms appear three to fourteen days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. And they typically last for between four and seven days. “There is no treatment for dengue fever or dengue hemorrhagic fever, but quick recognition and management of symptoms and complications is effective at preventing deaths.” Related stories Get closer to the game! content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue fever outbreak reaches 190 cases. Where it is spreading Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 25, 2026, 10:22 a.m. ET Florida's dengue count is approaching the highest level seen in recent years. A major outbreak of locally acquired cases are confirmed in Hillsborough County, in the Tampa Bay area. See breakdown of dengue by county. An outbreak of dengue continues in the Tampa Bay area on Florida's west coast. Of Florida's 190 locally acquired cases of dengue as of Sept. 19, 170 have been in Hillsborough County. The remainder are scattered in five other counties in the state, mostly in South Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health. The numbers are close to the highest number in recent memory, 199 in 2023, and far higher than the 62 cases reported in all of 2025. ➤ How worried should Florida residents, visitors be about dengue? Currently, 11 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents Here's where dengue has been reported in Florida, along with symptoms to watch for. Hillsborough County leads Florida with 170 cases of dengue fever According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 19, there have been 190 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in six counties, which is up from 152 reported Sept. 12. Of the 190 cases of locally acquired dengue, 170 were in Hillsborough County, according to the Florida Department of Health. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The county is under a mosquito-borne illness alert, according to an Aug. 12 alert update from the Hillsborough County Department of Health after the eighth case of locally acquired dengue was reported. Property owners can request a free on-site inspection from Mosquito Management Services Unit to have an inspection on their property to identify potential mosquito breeding sites. "If you feel that your neighborhood is a good candidate for mosquito spraying, you can fill out the form for a Neighborhood Spray Request. The county's mosquito spraying map shows areas sprayed within the last 28 days by both truck and aerial. 7 cases of dengue reported in Miami-Dade County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Miami-Dade County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue. Miami-Dade County said residents "experiencing significant mosquito problems can submit a service request online for an inspection" or call 311. 7 cases of dengue reported in Pinellas County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pinellas County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 11 after two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue. 3 cases of dengue reported in Orange County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been three cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Orange County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Sept. 2 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue was confirmed in the Pine Hills area and upgraded it to a mosquito-borne illness alert Sept. 18 after two additional confirmed cases of dengue were reported in the Apopka area, according to Orange County Mosquito Control. "Mosquito control crews are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in the affected areas and across the county to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." Orange County is also under a mosquito-borne illness advisory for West Nile virus. 2 cases of dengue reported in Pasco County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been two cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pasco County. "Dengue virus has become an increasingpublic-health concern in the Greater Tampa Bay region," Pasco County Mosquito Control posted on its website. "Because our region is so interconnected, this is not simply a Hillsborough County issue or a Pasco County issue. Thousands of people travel between Pasco, Hillsborough, Pinellas, Hernando, Citrus and surrounding counties every day for work, school, healthcare, recreation and other activities. "Reducing dengue transmission wherever it is occurring in the Tampa Bay region helps reduce the opportunity for the virus to be carried into neighboring communities." 1 case of dengue reported in Palm Beach County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been one case of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Department of Health issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue fever. Residents can use an online form to report mosquito activity. Palm Beach County Mosquito Control will "verify and document the presence of a legitimate mosquito problem" before spraying. What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? "The surge in dengue cases — along with a few West Nile and the first chikungunya — in Florida is chiefly driven by a combination of climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. The factors that creating ideal conditions for the mosquitoes responsible for transmitting the viruses include: Warmer temperatures: Summer high temperatures speed up mosquito life cycles and virus replication, allowing more mosquito generations in a single season and able to transmit viruses faster. Increased rainfall and standing water: Heavy rains and storm‐water runoff create abundant mosquito production sites in both natural and artificial containers. Outbreaks worldwide and human travel: Locations worldwide where Aedes aegypti-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya are endemic (experience transmission every year usually year-round) are experiencing outbreaks, Buckner said. What's the difference between a mosquito-borne illness advisory and alert? "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient Cheryl McCloud is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. TAK-003 reduced dengue hospitalizations, but protection varied by viral serotype. Vaccination decisions depend on local transmission, eligibility, and continued surveillance. DENGUE vaccines can reduce illness and hospitalization, but prior infection and viral serotype still shape protection. A narrative review of clinical trials, long-term follow-up, and regulatory evidence found that vaccine selection remains closely tied to baseline dengue exposure and local transmission. The question has growing relevance beyond traditionally endemic regions. The review describes expanding Aedes mosquito habitats and reports locally acquired dengue in parts of the United States. For clinicians, travel history remains important, but its absence does not rule out local exposure where transmission occurs. Why Prior Infection Matters Four distinct dengue virus serotypes complicate vaccine development. Infection with one serotype provides lasting protection against that serotype but limited protection against the others. An immune response that does not reliably neutralize a subsequent infection may contribute to antibody-dependent enhancement and more severe disease. That concern shaped use of CYD-TDV, the first authorized dengue vaccine. Its use was restricted to people with documented previous dengue infection after an increased risk of hospitalization and severe dengue emerged in some recipients who had never been infected. Baseline serostatus is therefore a clinical safety consideration, not simply a predictor of efficacy. Trial Results Reveal Uneven Protection In a Phase III trial involving more than 20,000 children and adolescents, two doses of TAK-003 were 73.3% effective against virologically confirmed dengue and 80.2% effective against dengue-related hospitalization during the first year after vaccination. At 4.5 years, the corresponding overall estimates were 61.2% and 84.1%. Protection against some serotypes remains less certain in people without prior dengue infection. A separate Brazilian Phase III trial found that one dose of Butantan-DV was 79.6% effective against symptomatic dengue over two years. Evidence was drawn mainly from periods when serotypes 1 and 2 circulated. The review also notes serious adverse event reports during its rollout; a causal relationship had not been established, and investigation was ongoing. Where Dengue Vaccination Fits The review favors population vaccination where dengue transmission and severe disease burden are sustained. In settings with sporadic transmission, it favors selective assessment based on exposure, previous infection, regulatory indications, and vaccine availability. It concludes that vaccination should accompany mosquito control, case surveillance, clinical preparedness, and continued monitoring of vaccine safety and effectiveness. Reference Esposito S and Principi N. Dengue vaccines in a changing epidemiological landscape: current evidence, unresolved challenges, and public health considerations. Vaccines. 2026;14(9):729. 29 September 2026 • In Focus Can Tarique Rahman’s plan break the Rohingya repatriation deadlock? 28 September 2026 • Geopolitical Insights DENGUE OUTBREAK DENV-3 now dominant strain Say experts; hospitals report rising admissions Updated : 4 August 2026, 08:31 • BANGLADESH SHARE Helemul Alam Helemul Alam Unable to find a seat, a woman sits on the floor with her child at Mugda Medical College Hospital in Dhaka. The child has had a fever for four days, and doctors suspect dengue while awaiting test results. According to the DGHS, at least three people died and 580 others were hospitalised with dengue in the 24 hours until 8:00am yesterday, taking this year’s death toll to 59 and total cases to 16,684. PHOTO: MEHEDI HASAN The DENV-3 serotype has become the dominant strain of the dengue virus in Bangladesh this year, replacing DENV-2, which was the most prevalent last year, according to the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR). A recent IEDCR survey of 71 dengue-positive patients found that 65 (91.55 percent) were infected with DENV-3, while the remaining six (9.23 percent) had DENV-2. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source By comparison, last year’s surveillance found DENV-2 in 49.2 percent of samples, followed by DENV-3 (35.8 percent), DENV-1 (8.8 percent), and DENV-4 (6.3 percent), IEDCR Director Dr Quazi Ahmed Zaki told The Daily Star. According to dengue experts, the virus has four serotypes -- DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4 -- each comprising several genotypes. Although DENV-2 has historically been linked to major outbreaks, disease severity depends on multiple factors rather than the serotype alone. Zaki cautioned against describing any serotype as inherently more dangerous. “It would not be scientifically accurate to label one dengue serotype as more severe on its own. Disease severity depends on factors including the viral strain, the patient’s immune response, and underlying illnesses,” he said. Zaki said the distribution of serotypes also varies across the country. “Samples from Dhaka and other urban healthcare facilities are different from those collected in the hill tracts and other rural areas,” he said. Image “The overall picture is mixed. Urban areas may show a higher concentration of one serotype, but you cannot generalise the findings for the entire country,” he said. The IEDCR director said previous dengue infection remains one of the strongest risk factors for severe disease. “People who have had dengue before face a higher risk of severe complications, including dengue shock syndrome, if they are infected again,” he said. Patients with kidney disease, liver disease, cancer, or other active infections are also at greater risk of severe illness, regardless of the infecting serotype or whether it is their first dengue infection, he added. He urged public awareness campaigns to focus on repeat infections and underlying health conditions rather than portraying one serotype as universally more dangerous. According to the Directorate General of Health Services, 59 people had died from dengue and 16,684 had been hospitalised this year as of August 3. Meanwhile, physicians say dengue admissions have increased sharply over the past two weeks. HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, said the hospital has opened two dedicated dengue wards -- one for male and the other for female patients -- after admissions rose to 15-20 patients in each admission cycle. Referring to the latest survey, he said both DENV-2 and DENV-3 are circulating this season, although DENV-3 appears to be more common. Among the four serotypes, DENV-2 and DENV-3 are more severe, Nazmul said. However, the risk of death is higher if a person who previously had dengue is infected with a different serotype, he added. He said many patients are going into shock rapidly, but clinicians have become more experienced in managing severe dengue. For all latest news, follow The Daily Star's Google News channel. “We are seeing patients who deteriorate quite quickly. However, management has improved, and most patients are receiving timely treatment,” he said. Doctors are also reporting a rise in dengue patients with hepatitis this year. “We are seeing considerably more dengue patients with hepatitis than in previous years. Some patients are also dealing with cardiac complications,” he said. He explained that dengue-associated hepatitis requires more than routine fluid management. “When dengue causes hepatitis and liver enzyme levels become markedly elevated, treatment has to be adjusted. These patients require closer monitoring and additional medications beyond standard dengue management,” he said. Ahsan urged people with persistent fever or warning signs to seek medical care promptly, saying early diagnosis and timely treatment remain the best way to prevent severe complications and deaths. content: Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One app. Start reading Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One news app. Start reading Medical Daily Elena Vega Sep 28, 2026, 12:40 PM Florida Local Dengue Cases Reach 190 as Hillsborough Declares Emergency and September Infections Show Mosquito Spread Continuing Florida Hillsborough CDC Hillsborough County Newsweek Pinellas the Florida Department of Health Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments in Florida's 2026 locally acquired dengue outbreak. State case figures come from the Florida Department of Health's Week 37 report, with data through Sept. 19, 2026. Hillsborough County declared a state of local emergency on Sept. 24. Numbers may change as the state releases more weekly reports and completes case investigations. Florida reported 38 new cases of locally acquired dengue in its latest weekly surveillance report, bringing the state's 2026 total to 190. The cases span six counties, and 30 of them began in September, according to the Florida Department of Health's Week 37 arbovirus report , which covers Sept. 13 to 19. Locally acquired means the person was infected by a mosquito in Florida, not while traveling. That distinction matters for anyone who gets sick without a recent trip, because neither the patient nor a clinician may think of dengue unless someone raises the possibility. Hillsborough County accounts for 170 of the 190 cases, or nearly nine in 10. The September onsets show that transmission did not stop in August, so households in affected counties still have reason to watch for fever and mention possible mosquito exposure when they seek care. Transmission Continued Into September The state counted 170 cases in Hillsborough, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas, three in Orange, two in Pasco, and one in Palm Beach. By the date symptoms started, 21 cases began in July, 139 in August, and 30 so far in September. The September count is likely to rise. Symptoms start before a person is tested and the case is reported, so illnesses that began in late September may not appear until later reports. The report also counted 17 mosquito pools, or batches of trapped mosquitoes, that tested positive this year. "In 2026, 190 cases of locally acquired dengue and 17 mosquito pools have been reported from six counties," the department wrote. Dengue is caused by four related virus types. Of the 171 cases that were typed, 169 were DENV-2, and two were DENV-3. The state also reported 212 travel-associated dengue cases this year, up from 186 in the prior report, plus one locally acquired chikungunya case in Miami-Dade with onset in August. Duval, Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts. Illness Without Travel History Dengue spreads mainly through the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. It does not spread through ordinary contact between people. Because dengue cases diagnosed in Florida are usually linked to travel, a fever in someone who has not left the state may not immediately suggest dengue. Kristi Miley, a researcher at the University of South Florida's Center for Global Health Infectious Disease Research, told Newsweek that "The Bay Area has seen more locally acquired cases than in previous years, indicating a localized outbreak in Hillsborough County's mosquito population rather than a statewide increase." She added that Hillsborough "has not recorded this level of dengue infection since the 1930s." "Many people may not seek care and fully recover without incidence; however it can be life-threatening for some, " Miley said. The CDC estimates that only about one in four people infected with dengue get sick, so official counts likely understate how many people have been infected. That is why telling a clinician about mosquito bites or living in an affected county matters, even without travel. Common symptoms include fever with aches and pains, such as pain behind the eyes or muscle, joint, or bone pain, along with nausea, vomiting, or rash. Symptoms typically last two to seven days, according to the CDC's dengue symptoms page . About one in 20 people who get sick develop severe dengue, a medical emergency. Warning Signs After the Fever Breaks Warning signs of severe dengue usually begin in the 24 to 48 hours after a fever goes away, when people may assume they are recovering. The CDC lists belly pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the nose or gums, vomiting blood or blood in the stool, and feeling extremely tired or restless as signs that require emergency care. Medication choices also matter. The CDC's dengue treatment guidance advises taking acetaminophen for fever and pain and warns, "Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen!" Those drugs can raise the risk of bleeding. According to a CDC health advisory , people at higher risk of severe dengue include infants, pregnant women, adults 65 and older, people with certain medical conditions, and people who have had a previous dengue infection and get infected again. Emergency Declaration Follows Weeks of Growth MedicalDaily previously reported that Florida's local dengue count had reached 152 , with Tampa Bay accounting for nearly all infections and 41 new cases in the prior week, the largest weekly increase this year. The newest data mark the third straight week with at least 38 new local cases, following 38 in Week 35 and 41 in Week 36. Hillsborough rose from 134 to 170 cases. Newsweek, citing the Tampa Bay Times, reported that an 80-year-old Hillsborough County woman died of dengue complications on Sept. 4, the state's first dengue death of 2026. The Florida Department of Health later confirmed the death. On Sept. 24, Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise signed an order declaring a state of local emergency over dengue . The order lasts seven days unless it is extended or rescinded, and it lets officials act quickly and seek federal reimbursement for certain costs. The county is conducting aerial mosquito treatments in several neighborhoods. Pasco and Pinellas counties declared their own local states of emergency the same week, and the Florida Department of Health in Polk County announced the county's first locally acquired case on Sept. 24. That case is not included in the Week 37 count. Practical protection has not changed. Residents should empty and scrub, turn over, cover, or throw out items that hold water, such as flowerpot saucers, buckets, pet bowls, toys, and tarps, at least once a week. They should also use EPA-registered insect repellent and keep window screens in good repair. The state releases arbovirus reports weekly, and the next update will show whether September cases keep climbing. For now, a fever after mosquito bites in an affected county is reason to call a clinician and mention dengue, whether or not the person has traveled. Key Questions Answered How many locally acquired dengue cases has Florida reported in 2026? There were 190 as of the Week 37 report, with data through Sept. 19, including 38 new cases that week. What does locally acquired mean? The person was infected by a mosquito in Florida rather than while traveling outside the state or country. Which counties have local cases? Hillsborough (170), Miami-Dade (7), Pinellas (7), Orange (3), Pasco (2), and Palm Beach (1). Is dengue still spreading? Yes. Thirty cases had September onset dates, and that number may rise as reports catch up. Polk County also announced its first local case on Sept. 24. What warning signs need emergency care? Belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, or extreme tiredness or restlessness, especially in the day or two after the fever fades. Which pain relievers should people avoid? The CDC advises acetaminophen and warns against aspirin and ibuprofen, which can increase bleeding risk. A recent death in Florida highlights the importance of recognizing symptoms and warning signs of severe dengue. The Florida Department of Health confirmed on Sept. 18, 2026, that the death of an elderly woman on Sept. 4 was due to dengue fever. It is the first confirmed dengue death in Hillsborough County, where health officials have reported multiple acquired cases. In August, the Hillsborough County Health Department issued a mosquito-borne illness alert. This cluster of locally spread cases is a stark reminder that a disease which most Americans associate with faraway tropical vacations is increasingly being caught at home. Dengue is often called “breakbone fever,” and the nickname is earned. People who get sick typically develop a sudden high fever along with a pounding headache, pain behind the eyes and deep aches in the muscles, joints and bones. Many also feel nauseated, throw up or break out in a blotchy rash a few days in. As an infectious diseases physician and tropical medicine specialist who directs a travel clinic, I see how easily dengue slips past both patients and doctors. In parts of the U.S. where the disease is still uncommon, it is easily mistaken for the flu or COVID-19, and that delay can be dangerous. How it spreads Dengue is not passed from person to person like a cold. It spreads through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti, a species commonly found in Florida. These mosquitoes thrive in warm cities and can breed in as little as a bottle capful of standing water. These mosquitoes bite during the day, not just at dusk. The cycle is simple and hard to break: A mosquito bites an infected person, then bites someone else days later, giving them the virus. Dengue is especially tricky because most infections cause no symptoms at all. Roughly 3 in 4 people who catch the virus never feel sick. For the 25% who are symptomatic, those symptoms don’t appear until four to 10 days after being bitten. In addition, there are four different strains of the dengue virus, and surviving one gives you lasting protection against only that one. A second infection with a different type actually raises the odds of severe disease. A life-threatening turn Most people suffer with dengue for a miserable week and then recover on their own. But about 1 in 20 patients progress to severe dengue, a life-threatening turn that tends to strike just as the fever breaks – often around days three to seven, when patients and their families may wrongly assume the worst is over. In severe dengue, tiny blood vessels throughout the body start leaking fluid, blood pressure can crash and dangerous bleeding or organ damage can follow. Warning signs that someone is sliding into this phase include severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, extreme drowsiness or restlessness, and blood in vomit or stool. Some groups face higher risk, including infants, pregnant women, adults over 65 and people with conditions like diabetes, obesity or kidney disease. Left untreated, severe dengue can kill up to 10% of patients. With prompt hospital care, that number drops below 1 in 100 – which is why recognizing it early matters so much. A dengue vaccine exists, but it is not recommended for the average American traveler. The available shots are used only in select cases, such as children who live in high-transmission areas and have already had dengue once. So prevention still rests mostly on avoiding mosquito bites. How dengue is treated There is no antiviral drug that cures dengue. Care is all about supporting the body while it fights the virus. For people well enough to stay home, that means rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known in the U.S. by the brand name Tylenol, for fever and pain. Patients who may have dengue must avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. These drugs raise the risk of bleeding, which is already a danger with dengue. Patients who develop more severe symptoms need to be admitted to the hospital, where doctors give carefully measured intravenous fluids and watch closely. Too little fluid and the patient can go into shock; too much and the lungs can flood. A worsening global problem Dengue is surging worldwide. The World Health Organization recorded more than 14 million cases in 2024, its worst year on record, across some 100 countries. That’s a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases reported in 2000. Warmer temperatures, rapid urban growth and global travel are all helping the mosquitoes – and the virus – expand into places where it has never been a problem before. South Asia, Southeast Asia and Latin America carry the heaviest burden, but the map is spreading north. Why the U.S. should pay attention Most U.S. dengue cases are still picked up abroad. Travelers return home sick. In 2023 alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such travel-related cases. But every infected traveler is a spark, and in warm states the tinder is already there. In the U.S. territories, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands see the most cases by far. Florida has the highest risk among the 50 states, with Miami-Dade County recording more than 300 locally acquired dengue infections between 2010 and 2024. Local cases have also turned up in Texas, California, Arizona and Hawaii. What to do if you think you have dengue If you develop a sudden fever after traveling to a dengue-prone area, or after mosquito exposure in South Florida, see a doctor and mention where you’ve been. Rest, drink fluids and use acetaminophen – not ibuprofen or aspirin. Most importantly, watch for the warning signs. Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or sudden drowsiness means get to an emergency room right away. And to protect yourself and your neighbors: Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and dump out any standing water in your yard where mosquitoes breed. This article originally appeared in The Conversation. Key Points Dengue is increasingly being transmitted locally in the U.S. Most infections cause no symptoms, while some can progress to severe disease. Severe dengue can emerge as a fever begins to subside. Florida currently faces the greatest risk among the 50 states. Why did Florida counties declare dengue emergencies? topics: Dengue Florida Local emergency Mosquito control Aedes aegypti Aedes albopictus Hillsborough Pasco WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (CBS12) — Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, prompting three counties to declare local states of emergency over the mosquito-borne disease. Pasco County declared a local state of emergency Sept. 23. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties followed the next day. The declarations allow local officials to bolster mosquito-control efforts and access emergency resources. Each declaration must be renewed to remain in effect beyond seven days. The latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report shows 190 locally acquired dengue cases statewide this year across six counties. Hillsborough County accounts for 170 cases, followed by Miami-Dade and Pinellas with seven each, Orange with three, Pasco with two and Palm Beach County with one. The report covers cases with onset through Sept. 19. Dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. It can cause flu-like symptoms, including aches and pains, nausea, vomiting and rash. In severe cases, it can lead to internal bleeding, shock and death. Event in Progress Newswise Live - Expert Spotlight Newswise Live - Events Scientific Meetings View all Meeting, Grants & Events Channels Sign up for the wires and see archived wires Sign Up Now Experts Expert Pitch Browse experts available to comment on breaking news Expert Query Request an expert contact, get responses directly to your inbox Expert Directory Find an expert by topic in a comprehensive database Journalists Pricing About About Curious by Nature Podcast Member Services Pricing Accessibility Statement Newswise Live Invoice Lookup Archived Wires Media Subscribers Services for Journalists Sample Effectiveness Reports Terms of Service Privacy Policy Our Staff Contact Us Blog FAQ Help ⌕ Request a Demo Login Register Expert Pitch Mosquito expert available to discuss Florida's dengue fever outbreak 30-Sep-2026 at 11:25 AM EDT, by Tulane University ♡ Credit: (Photo by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases on Unsplash) The two main species of Aedes mosquitoes that are capable of transmitting dengue — Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus — are recognizable by their black and white banding. Florida is experiencing one of its most significant dengue fever outbreaks in years, with case numbers rising statewide and the state's first virus-related death confirmed by the Florida Department of Health in early September. "It's one of the worst years for dengue that Florida has had in some time," said Tulane University medical entomologist Dawn Wesson. "They'll have a few locally transmitted cases most years, but not this many. It's also a little unique in that it's further north than where most previous outbreaks have hit, which tend to be closer to the Miami-Dade area." Wesson, who directs Tulane's Vector-Borne Infectious Disease Initiative and has studied dengue and other vector-borne viruses for more than three decades, said the outbreak is being driven by a combination of climate and human travel that allow Aedes mosquitoes to thrive and spread the virus. "Part of it is climate," said Wesson, associate professor of tropical medicine at Tulane’s Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public Health and Tropical Medicine. "But it's also that people travel all over the world, and people coming into airports like Miami disperse into the surrounding area, and some of them are infected with dengue. They bring the virus in and set off local transmission.” Two Aedes species spread dengue: Aedes aegypti, the primary vector, which originated in Africa, and Aedes albopictus, the Tiger mosquito, native to Southeast Asia, which is believed to have arrived in the U.S. in the mid-1980s in shipments of used scrap tires. Unlike many mosquitoes found in the U.S., Aedes bite during the day and are recognizable by their black-and-white banded markings. They lay their eggs in natural containers like tree holes as well as man-made ones such as tires. “Tires tend to be a real problem for all these container-inhabiting mosquitoes,” Wesson added. Wesson said the mosquitoes are especially difficult to control and current tools remain limited. Medical entomologists like Wesson are pursuing ways to kill them outright or alter them genetically or bacterially so they can't transmit the virus as well. "That's the kind of stuff that keeps me up at night and keeps me busy," Wesson said. Wesson has traveled the world researching new tools to fight dengue, including projects in South America, and has served in advisory roles with local parish and regional mosquito control boards. For everyday protection from mosquitoes, Wesson recommends DEET-based repellent as well as long sleeves and a hat. Dengue outbreaks are also surging elsewhere in the world, including a major outbreak currently ongoing in Bangladesh. In the U.S., locally acquired dengue cases have also been reported in Hawaii, Texas, California and Arizona in past years. Key takeaways: Locally acquired cases of the mosquito-borne illness have shifted from its traditional footprint of South Florida. “I am really concerned about this,” an expert said. Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency due to a surge in locally acquired dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness that has circulated in Florida for years. But unlike previous dengue outbreaks in the state, which were mostly centered in South Florida, the numbers show a new trend for 2026: The viral illness is moving north, specifically to the state’s central Gulf Coast. The Florida Department of Health has confirmed a total of 190 locally acquired cases of dengue, a mosquito-borne illness, in 2026. Source: James Gathany/CDC “What’s happening here is something different,” Nicole Iovine , MD, PhD, chief hospital epidemiologist at UF Health Shands Hospital in Gainesville, Florida, told Healio. “We always see some local acquisition of dengue — typically in South Florida. What's so notable now is that it made a jump north to the Tampa area.” The Florida Department of Health has confirmed a total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases as of Sept. 19 — 170 of those in Hillsborough County, which encompasses Tampa. Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas counties declared local states of emergency this month in response to the dengue surge. Last year, Hillsborough reported just one such case. Florida has also recorded 212 travel-associated dengue cases in 2026. But it is the amount of locally acquired dengue cases in the state that has exploded, already tripling last year’s count of 62, and surpassing Florida's recent peak of 176 set in 2023. “I am really concerned about this,” Iovine said. Moreover, this year’s El Niño weather pattern should extend warm, wet weather through the winter and keep dengue-carrying mosquitoes alive, Iovine said. “That’s just going to increase the threat because mosquitoes will be around for the winter potentially, as opposed to being killed off by a few days of a cold, hard freeze, like we normally hope for,” she said. Dengue is known as “break-bone fever” because of the crushing aches and pains it can cause for some people in the joints, legs and back, the CDC notes. “It feels like your bones are breaking, which is hard to imagine what that must feel like,” Iovine said. “These patients feel miserable.” Other symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting and a rash, according to the CDC. Severe cases occur in around 5% of people and can be life-threatening within a few hours, the agency notes. Florida health officials have reported one dengue-related death this year — an 80-year-old Tampa woman who died on Sept. 4, according to the Tampa Bay Times . Dengue virus is transmitted to people via the bite of an infected Aedes species mosquito, primarily Aedes aegypti , according to the CDC. It is common in tropical and subtropical areas worldwide. WHO estimates that around half the world’s population is at risk for dengue. The surge in Florida comes on the heels of the discontinuation of the only dengue vaccine ever licensed for use in the U.S. The FDA approved the vaccine, Dengvaxia, in 2019 for children aged 9 to 16 years living in U.S. territories where dengue is endemic, including American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. But the vaccine, which is complicated to administer and available only to children with a confirmed previous dengue infection, was pulled from the market by Sanofi Pasteur because of a lack of demand. “The good news is we know how to make a vaccine — that's kind of the first big step that's already been done,” Iovine said. “It'll be very interesting to watch in the pharmaceutical space to see whether or not any decisions will now be made to bring (the vaccine) back to market.” Another dengue vaccine manufactured by Takeda is available in other countries outside the U.S. Takeda voluntarily pulled its FDA application for the vaccine in 2023 after the agency cited a lack of data that it protects against all four dengue serotypes. TICK-BORNE ‘RABBIT FEVER’ SPREADS WITH CASES REPORTED NEAR MAJOR METRO AREA Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES “The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida,” an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health, makers of OFF!, said in a statement sent to Fox News Digital. “As dengue cases continue to be reported in the Tampa area, taking steps to help prevent mosquito bites is especially important,” the expert went on. “Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk.” The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) previously said crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to reports. FMCA has urged residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health entomologist shared the following recommendations to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne disease. The FMCA also advises people to dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors. Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition. Symptoms typically begin four to 10 days after the bite of an infected mosquito. Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness. People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care. ON AIR NOW On Air Now Joe Pags 6:00 PM - 9:00 PM WFMD LISTENER CLUB FACEBOOK

content: News Sports Restaurants Real Estate Opinion Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue fever outbreak reaches 190 cases. Where it is spreading Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 25, 2026, 10:22 a.m. ET Florida's dengue count is approaching the highest level seen in recent years. A major outbreak of locally acquired cases are confirmed in Hillsborough County, in the Tampa Bay area. See breakdown of dengue by county. An outbreak of dengue continues in the Tampa Bay area on Florida's west coast. Of Florida's 190 locally acquired cases of dengue as of Sept. 19, 170 have been in Hillsborough County. The remainder are scattered in five other counties in the state, mostly in South Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health. The numbers are close to the highest number in recent memory, 199 in 2023, and far higher than the 62 cases reported in all of 2025. ➤ How worried should Florida residents, visitors be about dengue? Currently, 11 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents Here's where dengue has been reported in Florida, along with symptoms to watch for. Hillsborough County leads Florida with 170 cases of dengue fever According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 19, there have been 190 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in six counties, which is up from 152 reported Sept. 12. Of the 190 cases of locally acquired dengue, 170 were in Hillsborough County, according to the Florida Department of Health. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The county is under a mosquito-borne illness alert, according to an Aug. 12 alert update from the Hillsborough County Department of Health after the eighth case of locally acquired dengue was reported. Property owners can request a free on-site inspection from Mosquito Management Services Unit to have an inspection on their property to identify potential mosquito breeding sites. "If you feel that your neighborhood is a good candidate for mosquito spraying, you can fill out the form for a Neighborhood Spray Request. The county's mosquito spraying map shows areas sprayed within the last 28 days by both truck and aerial. 7 cases of dengue reported in Miami-Dade County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Miami-Dade County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue. Miami-Dade County said residents "experiencing significant mosquito problems can submit a service request online for an inspection" or call 311. 7 cases of dengue reported in Pinellas County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pinellas County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 11 after two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue. 3 cases of dengue reported in Orange County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been three cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Orange County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Sept. 2 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue was confirmed in the Pine Hills area and upgraded it to a mosquito-borne illness alert Sept. 18 after two additional confirmed cases of dengue were reported in the Apopka area, according to Orange County Mosquito Control. "Mosquito control crews are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in the affected areas and across the county to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." Orange County is also under a mosquito-borne illness advisory for West Nile virus. 2 cases of dengue reported in Pasco County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been two cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pasco County. "Dengue virus has become an increasingpublic-health concern in the Greater Tampa Bay region," Pasco County Mosquito Control posted on its website. "Because our region is so interconnected, this is not simply a Hillsborough County issue or a Pasco County issue. Thousands of people travel between Pasco, Hillsborough, Pinellas, Hernando, Citrus and surrounding counties every day for work, school, healthcare, recreation and other activities. "Reducing dengue transmission wherever it is occurring in the Tampa Bay region helps reduce the opportunity for the virus to be carried into neighboring communities." 1 case of dengue reported in Palm Beach County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been one case of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Department of Health issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue fever. Residents can use an online form to report mosquito activity. Palm Beach County Mosquito Control will "verify and document the presence of a legitimate mosquito problem" before spraying. What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? "The surge in dengue cases — along with a few West Nile and the first chikungunya — in Florida is chiefly driven by a combination of climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. The factors that creating ideal conditions for the mosquitoes responsible for transmitting the viruses include: Warmer temperatures: Summer high temperatures speed up mosquito life cycles and virus replication, allowing more mosquito generations in a single season and able to transmit viruses faster. Increased rainfall and standing water: Heavy rains and storm‐water runoff create abundant mosquito production sites in both natural and artificial containers. Outbreaks worldwide and human travel: Locations worldwide where Aedes aegypti-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya are endemic (experience transmission every year usually year-round) are experiencing outbreaks, Buckner said. What's the difference between a mosquito-borne illness advisory and alert? "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient Cheryl McCloud is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient Cheryl McCloud is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. claims six more lives, death toll rises to 239 Bangladesh Battles Severe Dengue Outbreak, Fatalities Reach 239 in 2023 T The Hawk· 🏷 Sep 29, 2026, 09:15 PM(Updated Oct 01, 2026, 02:06 AM) Discover more Online news portal Digital news access Epaper access pass Dhaka, Sep 29 (IANS) As many as six people died due to dengue in Bangladesh in the 24 hours until 8 am (local time) on Tuesday, raising the fatalities from the mosquito-borne disease in 2026 to 239, local media reported. During the same period, 1,942 new dengue patients were admitted to hospitals in Bangladesh, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Among the total deaths, 52.9 per cent were women and 47.1 per cent men, United News of Bangladesh (UNB) reported. News subscription service As many as 77,672 dengue patients have been hospitalised in Bangladesh since January 1. Among them, 72,008 people have recovered from the mosquito-borne disease. As Bangladesh grapples with a worsening dengue outbreak, country's Prime Minister Tarique Rehman on September 6 ordered the authorities to increase cleanliness drives and public awareness campaigns to prevent the spread of dengue, UNB reported. Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV), which is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. There is no specific treatment for dengue and early detection and access to proper medical care lowers fatality rates of severe dengue. Bangladesh has reported a sharp increase in dengue deaths and cases in recent years compared with the 18 years from 2000-2018, local media reported. Bangladesh reported 296 dengue deaths and 50,208 cases from 2000 to 2018. In the following seven years and nine months, the fatalities from the mosquito-borne disease rose to 3,466 deaths and 7,86,091 cases, Bangladesh-based The Daily Star reported. The dengue deaths in Bangladesh were about 11.71 times the earlier figure, while reported cases were about 15.66 times higher. Public health expert Mushtuq Husain said that long-term, coordinated and people-centred public health programme was required for sustainable dengue control. Husain said Aedes mosquitoes had adapted to different environments and could breed even in small amounts of stagnant water and their spread was no longer confined to urban regions, The Daily Star reported. Husain stated that the increase in population and repeated infections were further complicating the situation. He further said that people who were previously infected with dengue could again contract the disease, while communities with little or no previous exposure are also reporting dengue infections. --IANS akl/as Continue reading BangladeshDenguePublic healthMosquito-borne diseaseOutbreakInfectious Disease About UsPrivacy PolicyContact UsEpaperNewslettersSitemap Powered by ZedBlu Tech Pvt. content: Epaper Daily Thanthi Thanthi TV Add as Preferred on Epaper Daily Thanthi Thanthi TV Chennai Tamil Nadu India World Entertainment Entertainment Cinema OTT Business Sports Lifestyle Technology Videos Explainers Editor's Picks Tamil Nadu Dengue & monsoon fevers in Tamil Nadu: Symptoms, testing, platelet count, warning signs & prevention Here are some key questions to help readers understand when to seek testing and medical attention. Amid a rise in dengue cases, the Tamil Nadu Health and Family Welfare Department has intensified surveillance across the StateJUSTIN Online Desk Updated on: 30 Sep 2026, 6:28 am Add DT Next as your Preferred Source.See our stories first in Google Search & Top Stories Add as Preferred Source Copied Follow Us Quick summary Through official health channels: Consult a doctor if you develop persistent fever or dengue-like symptoms → get the recommended dengue test based on the illness stage → monitor platelet counts and other blood parameters as advised → seek urgent care if warning signs such as severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or bleeding appear → prevent dengue by eliminating stagnant water and report mosquito-related concerns through the GCC’s 1913 helpline. CHENNAI: As monsoon-related illnesses increase, fever can often be difficult to identify by symptoms alone. Dengue, seasonal viral infections and other mosquito-borne diseases may initially appear similar. Here are some key questions to help readers understand when to seek testing and medical attention. ALSO READ Granite baron Veeramani booked under POSCO Act in suicide case What are the common symptoms of dengue? Dengue commonly begins with a sudden high fever. Other symptoms can include severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and skin rashes. However, these symptoms can overlap with other viral infections. A doctor may recommend a blood test to confirm dengue rather than relying on symptoms alone. How can dengue be different from a regular seasonal viral fever? There is no reliable way to distinguish dengue from every other viral fever based only on symptoms. Dengue may be suspected when high fever is accompanied by intense body or joint pain, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea or rash. Persistent or worsening symptoms should be medically evaluated, particularly during periods when dengue cases are circulating. Fever cases rise in Chennai, dengue surveillance intensified When should someone get tested for dengue? The appropriate test can depend on how many days the person has had symptoms. Tests that detect the dengue virus or its NS1 antigen are generally useful during the early stage of illness, while antibody testing becomes more useful later. A doctor can determine which test is appropriate based on the patient's symptoms and the stage of the illness. Where can people get free fever testing at government facilities in Chennai? Government healthcare facilities in Chennai provide services for people presenting with fever, including evaluation for dengue and other infections. The Greater Chennai Corporation's health facilities include Urban Primary Health Centres and diagnostic centres offering investigations. People should check with the particular government facility for its current testing availability and timings before visiting. Rising dengue cases put Tamil Nadu hospitals on alert Are dengue tests available free of cost at government centres? Diagnostic investigations are available free of cost at several Greater Chennai Corporation facilities. Availability can vary depending on the centre and the test required, so patients should confirm the service at the facility. What platelet count is considered dangerous in dengue? Platelet numbers are only one part of assessing a dengue patient's condition. A falling platelet count does not automatically mean that a platelet transfusion is required. A count below 10,000 platelets per microlitre is generally considered a level at which prophylactic platelet transfusion may be considered in dengue patients who do not have bleeding, according to India's national dengue management guidance. Active bleeding and the patient's overall clinical condition are also important factors. Patients should not attempt to interpret platelet reports on their own. Doctors may monitor platelet counts along with other blood parameters and signs of bleeding or plasma leakage. Dengue, fever cases on the rise in Chennai; Adyar, Anna Nagar, Valasaravakkam turn hotspots Does every dengue patient with low platelets need a platelet transfusion? No. A low platelet count by itself does not necessarily mean a transfusion is required. Clinical condition, bleeding and other complications are considered when deciding treatment. This is particularly important because platelet counts can fall during dengue and then recover as the patient improves. What are the warning signs that require urgent medical attention? Immediate medical assessment is important if a person with suspected or confirmed dengue develops symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stools, unusual drowsiness, extreme weakness or restlessness. The period around the time the fever comes down can also be critical, so improvement in temperature does not always mean the illness has passed. How can residents help prevent dengue in their neighbourhood? The dengue mosquito breeds in stagnant water. Residents should regularly empty or cover containers that can collect water, including buckets, pots, discarded tyres and other outdoor items. Keeping surroundings free of water accumulation can reduce mosquito breeding and help protect the wider community. Where can Chennai residents report stagnant water or mosquito-related concerns? Residents can report public-health and mosquito-related complaints to the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) through its civic grievance channels, including the 1913 helpline. Providing the exact location of stagnant water can help civic teams identify and address potential mosquito-breeding sites. What should someone do if they develop a fever during the monsoon? Do not assume that every monsoon fever is dengue or, conversely, that dengue can be ruled out because symptoms appear mild. People with persistent fever or symptoms suggestive of dengue should consult a healthcare professional and follow the recommended testing and monitoring schedule. Self-medication, particularly with medicines that can increase bleeding risk, should be avoided unless advised by a doctor. content: Skip to main content E-PAPER ARCHIVE Today's FE AUTO বাংলা Wednesday • 30 September 2026 Home Economy▾ Stock▾ Trade National▾ World▾ Editorial Views▾ More categories▾ Our Correspondent Published: Sep 27, 2026, 05:35 Share this news Country | 3 days ago Dengue outbreak takes a lethal turn in Rajshahi Dengue patients receiving treatment inside mosquito nets at Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH) in Rajshahi city amid a recent surge in infection of the deadly disease in the region. — FE Photo Infectious Diseases Our Correspondent Published: Sep 27, 2026, 05:35 RAJSHAHI, Sept 26: Dengue epidemic becomes critical in the Rajshahi region as patients are pouring into Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH) with severe complications, including dengue shock syndrome (DSS) and myocarditis. More than 25 new dengue patients are being admitted to the hospital on average every day. In several recent cases, patients' condition deteriorated rapidly and they died within hours of admission. According to RMCH data, dengue admissions began on June 7 this year, while deaths were first reported in August. As of Friday, 13 dengue patients died at the hospital, while a total of 901 patients had been admitted. Of the admitted patients, 833 were adults, including 610 men and 223 women, while 68 were children. A total of 802 patients have so far been discharged after treatment. The recent trend is particularly alarming. Eleven dengue patients died at RMCH between August 31 and September 25. Ten of them died from dengue shock syndrome, while one died from a dengue-related cardiac complication. The cases show how quickly severe dengue can turn fatal. On September 9, Pabna's Bera resident Imrul Kayes died just one and a half hours after being admitted to the hospital with dengue. The following day, college student Jeet Sarker of Bonpara in Natore died around 15 hours after admission. City & Local Guides Hridoy, a resident of Bholahat in Chapainawabganj, died on September 14 after being admitted the previous morning. The next day, housewife Asma Khatun of Balubagan in Chapainawabganj died after being admitted the previous evening. Tanore resident Anwar Mondal died about eight hours after admission on September 18. School student Sathi Rani of Bagmara, who was admitted on September 19, died early the following morning. Abdul Karim of Battala Hat in Chapainawabganj died on September 21 after five days of treatment. Nasrin, a working woman from Sultannabad in Rajshahi city, died on September 24, four days after being admitted. Doctors say dengue shock syndrome is one of the most serious complications of dengue. Excessive plasma leakage from blood vessels reduces the effective volume of circulating blood, causing a sharp fall in blood pressure and impairing blood flow to vital organs. Without timely treatment, the patient's condition can deteriorate rapidly. Myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, is another complication drawing concern among doctors. It can affect the heart's normal function and may cause a rapid deterioration in the patient's condition. Doctors at RMCH say delayed hospitalisation is one of the major concerns behind the recent deaths. Many patients initially treat fever at home or seek local treatment, assuming it to be a common viral infection. They often reach the hospital only after serious complications have developed. Medical Facilities & Services RMCH spokesperson Dr Sheikh Shamim Ahmed said many patients were arriving at the hospital at a very advanced stage because they were ignoring fever or spending valuable time on local treatment. "When patients develop complications such as dengue shock syndrome or myocarditis, it becomes difficult to save them even with treatment," he said. He advised people to consult a doctor as soon as fever develops and undergo an NS1 test when recommended. He also urged patients to seek immediate medical attention if they experience severe weakness, abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulties, unusual drowsiness or reduced urine output. Meanwhile, the Rajshahi City Corporation (RCC) says it has intensified its mosquito-control activities across the city. Cleaning drives, destruction of potential Aedes breeding sites and mosquito-control operations are being conducted in different wards. RCC chief cleanliness officer Sheikh MdMamun Dollar said the corporation's anti-dengue campaign was continuing across all wards, with greater emphasis on eliminating Aedes breeding sites. Rajshahi district entomologist Umme Habiba said Aedes larvae and adult mosquitoes were being found in common household containers and other small water-holding places. Hospitals & Treatment Centers Deputy Commissioner Kazi Shahidul Islam stressed prevention and community participation in containing the outbreak. "Stagnant water and an unclean environment create ideal conditions for Aedes breeding. Prevention must come before treatment. We need to remove stagnant water and destroy potential breeding sites around homes and other premises," he said. "As part of the three-month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign, cleanliness drives are being conducted simultaneously every Saturday at 78 locations across nine upazilas of the district," he said. anaetru@gmail.com Our Correspondent Published: Sep 27, 2026, 05:35 Share this news Our Correspondent Published: Sep 29, 2026, 04:03 Share this news Country | 1 day ago Tk 7.48b project, taken after 'worst' floods, delayed for a year in Sylhet A view of CC blocks for the FREAP project in Sylhet. — FE photo Health Conditions Our Correspondent Published: Sep 29, 2026, 04:03 SYLHET, Sept 28: Implementation of a Tk 7.48 billion project to protect about 80,000 hectares of farmland from early floods and restoration of infrastructure to facilitate water recession on those lands located in Sylhet's three divisions was delayed with the deadline extended a year till June 2027. The project was taken after devastating floods in these regions in 2022. Some of the project's schemes, which include restoring 103.73 km of flood control embankment and construction of 15 flood fuses, have not seen almost any development for more than the last two months. Improvement of submersible embankment by armouring through cement concrete (CC) blocks and five km river protection works are also part of the project titled 'Flood Reconstruction Emergency Assistance Project' (FREAP), which was completed over 80 per cent in Sunamganj, 75 per cent in Habiganj and 71 per cent in Sylhet, a government official said. Dipak Ranjan Das, executive engineer, Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), Sylhet, said some works on embankment and riverbank road could not be completed at the Sylhet-Assam frontiers in Zakiganj over the objection of India's Border Security Force. Stating that the project had been delayed for various reasons, Mr Das added that it is on the way towards completion within the new deadline. Sources in the government offices involved in the project said they are trying their best to complete the works within the updated deadline, which the FE understands that they intend to ensure completion within that deadline even if it slightly compromises quality. Infectious Diseases Probir Kumar Goshwami, additional chief engineer of north-east BWDB, said, "We would have to complete it in this fiscal as the progress is almost 80 per cent. It was taken after the greater Sylhet region and other haor districts suffered worst floods in 2022." The project is being implemented with significant financial support from the Asian Development Bank, while BWDB, Local Government Engineering Department, Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) and Bangladesh Railway have also being assisting. For instance, one of the responsibilities of the DAE includes managing solar plant installations in the project area, while Bangladesh Railway would plant trees. After major irregularities were found during an investigation in the Sunamganj section of the project in 2025, BWDB officials were penalised and transferred. Some contractors had delayed works and among them Messrs Jamil Iqbal had left after the July Revolution. forsylhet@gmail.com Our Correspondent Published: Sep 29, 2026, 04:03 Share this news

Prev Next Officials say so far they’ve found just one mosquito infected with dengue fever in Pasco County and two cases involving people. By: Erik Waxler Posted 9:32 PM, Sep 24, 2026 Erik Waxler is committed to covering the stories that matter to you in the Greater Pasco County area. If you have a story idea, please email Erik@TampaBay28.com ODESSA, FL (WFTS) — With dengue fever cases mounting in neighboring Hillsborough County, Pasco County officials say they are not waiting for transmission of the mosquito-borne virus to become widespread locally. Pasco County has declared a local state of emergency and is encouraging other Tampa Bay area communities to do the same. Pasco County Fighting Off Dengue Fever Hillsborough County also declared a state of local emergency. The concern is on the mind of people like Patty McCloskey, who was heading back to her car after a hike at Starkey Wilderness Preserve. “I love the outdoors and nature and just being out in the fresh air,” McCloskey said. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE She said she was aware of the rising number of mosquito-borne dengue cases. She also discovered she had been bitten while outdoors. “It makes you not want to be out in nature, but sometimes you take that chance,” McCloskey said. Pasco County officials say they have found one mosquito infected with dengue and have confirmed two cases involving people. But with nearly 200 cases reported in neighboring Hillsborough County and one confirmed dengue-related death, Pasco officials say they are taking steps now to try to prevent a larger outbreak. The county's local state of emergency is expected to make it easier to get additional resources from the state. “They’ll be able to send additional resources, equipment, people to help with boots on the ground, chemicals that are needed to help combat the mosquitoes, within not just Pasco, but hopefully within our Tampa Bay region,” Pasco County Commissioner Seth Weightman said. Pasco County has been preparing for the threat of dengue for years. Tampa Bay 28 visited the Pasco County Mosquito Control District lab two years ago to see how staff members were working to protect residents from the virus. At the time, Executive Director Adriane Rogers explained how severe dengue can become. “Dengue is nicknamed breakbone fever. In more severe cases, we actually have issues where you feel like your bones are breaking. It’s that severe,” Rogers said. Now, mosquito control crews are collecting and testing mosquito samples and spraying insecticide in areas where mosquitoes could potentially spread the virus. Pasco is also lending one of its two mosquito control helicopters to Hillsborough County to assist with spraying there. Pasco officials say controlling the outbreak requires a regional response and are encouraging neighboring counties to take similar emergency action. “The issue in Hillsborough County is great. And the issue needs to be taken care of in Hillsborough County,” Pasco's Mosquito Control District Commissioner Michael Cox said. Residents can also help reduce the mosquito population around their homes. Officials recommend regularly checking yards for containers and other areas that collect standing water, where mosquitoes can breed.
